Azure MySQL

Source: vignettes/azure-mysql.Rmd
azure-mysql.Rmd

Use oauth_db_azure_mysql() to query Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server with each Shiny visitor’s Microsoft account. MySQL checks their Entra identity and applies the privileges assigned to that user or group. The helper returns a DBI connection for SQL and dbplyr queries.

Set up access

Install the R package odbc and the 64-bit MariaDB Connector/ODBC driver on the machine running Shiny. Use Connector/ODBC 3.1 or later. Find its registered name with unique(odbc::odbcListDrivers()$name); driver names vary by installed version and operating system.

Ask your administrator to enable Entra authentication on the Flexible Server, configure an Entra administrator, and create MySQL users for the visitors or their groups. Grant those users access to your database and tables. The Shiny host also needs network access to the server.

Create an Entra Web app registration with http://localhost:8100 as its redirect URI. Follow the Microsoft registration steps, but select Azure OSSRDBMS Database and its delegated user_impersonation permission. Request admin consent if your tenant requires it. Save the registration settings in a local .Renviron and restart R:

OAUTHDB_TENANT_ID=your-tenant-id
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID=your-client-id
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET=your-client-secret

Get the PEM CA bundle recommended in Azure’s TLS configuration guide. The driver verifies the certificate chain and server hostname. Keep the bundle current as Azure rotates its certificates.

A complete app

Save this as example.R. Replace the server, database, MySQL user or group, driver name and CA bundle path with your settings:

library(shiny)
library(shinyOAuth)
library(shinyOAuthDB)

client <- oauth_db_microsoft_client(
  services = "mysql",
  tenant_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_TENANT_ID"),
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100"
)

ui <- oauth_ui(
  fluidPage(
    actionButton("login", "Sign in"),
    actionButton("logout", "Sign out"),
    tableOutput("rows")
  ),
  id = "auth",
  client = client
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  auth <- oauth_module_server("auth", client, auto_redirect = FALSE)
  observeEvent(input$login, auth$request_login())
  observeEvent(input$logout, auth$logout())

  con <- oauth_db_azure_mysql(
    auth$connection,
    server = "example.mysql.database.azure.com",
    database = "reporting",
    user = "reporting-readers",
    driver = "MariaDB ODBC 3.2 Driver",
    ssl_ca = "path/to/azure-ca.pem"
  )

  output$rows <- renderTable({
    connection <- con()
    DBI::dbGetQuery(
      connection,
      "SELECT CURRENT_USER() AS database_user, DATABASE() AS database_name"
    )
  })
}

runApp(
  shinyApp(ui, server, uiPattern = ".*"),
  port = 8100,
  launch.browser = FALSE
)

Run source("example.R"), then open http://localhost:8100 in your regular browser. Embedded RStudio/Positron viewers can’t complete the redirects. Sign in to see the MySQL identity and database; sign out to clear the output.

For a group account, set user to the exact group name provisioned in MySQL. Azure checks that the signed-in visitor belongs to that group. For individual accounts, supply a reactive function returning the provisioned MySQL name for the current identity. Don’t assume every tenant maps an email address to the same database name.

Query your tables

Call connection <- con() inside each reactive expression before using DBI. For values supplied by users, use bound parameters:

output$rows <- renderTable({
  connection <- con()
  DBI::dbGetQuery(
    connection,
    "SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE country = ? LIMIT 20",
    params = list("NL")
  )
})

You can also pass connection to dplyr::tbl() for dbplyr queries. MySQL database grants determine what the visitor can access. A group login uses that group’s grants; it doesn’t provide individual row filtering on its own.

Tokens and connections

The preset requests https://ossrdbms-aad.database.windows.net/.default when MySQL is the only service, and the explicit user_impersonation scope when combined with other Microsoft services. MySQL and Azure PostgreSQL share this resource audience, with separate named token targets mysql and postgres. An existing client can supply the same audience through a custom target; use target = NULL for a client without named targets.

The helper passes the access token as the password through mysql_clear_password over verified TLS. You don’t need an OpenID Connect driver plugin or a process-wide environment variable. MySQL Enterprise’s ID-token authentication is a different mechanism.

This helper uses MariaDB’s driver to connect to Azure’s MySQL server. MySQL Connector/ODBC 9.5 crashed during validation with credentials longer than its connection-option buffer. MariaDB Connector/ODBC accepted the 12 KB test token; the two drivers’ TLS settings are not interchangeable.

After shinyOAuth renews a token, the next call to con() opens a connection with the current token and closes the previous handle. This doesn’t rerun completed reactive queries, but it ends any transaction or temporary tables on the old connection. Obtain one handle for each operation and complete its transaction before returning control to Shiny.

The helper disables the driver’s automatic reconnect. If a query loses its connection, handle the failure, disconnect the broken native handle, and call con() before another query. It never automatically resubmits SQL. Sign-out, account or username changes, and session end close the connection.

Validation

Unit tests cover driver arguments, token renewal, account changes and permission loss. Local protocol checks can test the real ODBC driver’s cleartext authentication over TLS. They don’t establish Azure compatibility: before deployment, verify Entra consent, user/group mapping and denied access with two real Azure users.
